first.rationale: The objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, so verification capacity should go to the beliefs that are both decision-critical right now and weakest against that specific bar. memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the most tempting response to the competitor's entry pricing and would be the highest-commitment move, yet it is evidenced only by 'acquisition and revenue lift' with no durability, margin, or retention read — exactly the kind of proxy that can look like growth while importing low-willingness-to-pay accounts, resetting price expectations, and inviting a discount war we cannot win. That is a downstream value-erosion risk I am flagging explicitly, and it is why I will not commit the single slot to discounting on an unverified record. memory_86 is the second pull because onboarding is the direction I actually intend to run, and its stated outcomes (completion rate, time-to-value, 'early product adoption') are all upstream proxies; I need the original record to see whether shortened onboarding ever traced through to retained, qualified revenue or merely to accounts that completed a shorter form. I did not spend a pull on memory_57 (referral) because it already carries a retention-harm check and is not the top candidate this week, nor on memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist), which is not implicated by the SMB-side declines, nor on memory_91, which is a near-duplicate proxy claim to memory_86 and would buy less new information. Current intent: simplify_onboarding as a standard experiment. Onboarding completion is down 4% and activation down 6%, and these are plausibly the same funnel wound; onboarding is the upstream cause, it is under our control, it is corroborated by two independent memories (memory_31 and memory_86), and unlike discounting it does not mortgage future pricing power. I am holding this intent loosely: if the memory_73 archive shows durable, margin-preserving revenue rather than a one-quarter acquisition spike, promotional pricing becomes defensible; if the memory_86 archive shows the lift never survived past week one or came from a population unlike our current cohort, I drop to a small guarded test with revenue-quality instrumentation rather than a standard rollout. Both memories are inherited summaries whose consolidation has already stripped the caveats, so I am treating them as directionally reliable but not as settled fact.

final.rationale: Both pulls paid off, and in opposite directions. exp_73 vindicates the concern that motivated the pull: the +18% qualified revenue in the consolidated memory was real but came bundled with -12% 30-day retention, and the original record's own conclusion explicitly warns against generalizing targeted discounting as sustainable growth. The consolidation had stripped that warning entirely, leaving a summary that read as clean endorsement. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is now affirmatively ruled out, not merely deprioritized — matching the competitor's entry pricing would buy a cohort that does not survive its first renewal and would reset price expectations for the accounts we already keep. Losing some price-sensitive SMB accounts to the competitor is the cheaper outcome; those are disproportionately the accounts exp_73 shows we cannot retain anyway. exp_86 came back confirmed and, importantly, confirmed on the right terminal metric: completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days are proxies, but 30-day retention +3% shows the lift traced through to durable behavior rather than to a shorter form. That converts my provisional intent into a committed one and removes the reason I would have downgraded to a small guarded test. Corroboration from memory_31 (independent, day 12, same direction on SMB activation) further supports it. So: simplify_onboarding, standard experiment. Standard rather than broad because the confirming evidence is a single verified record from an earlier period and the current 4%/6% declines may have causes onboarding does not touch; standard rather than small because the evidence is stronger than anything else available and the slot does not carry over, so under-powering it wastes the week. Residual uncertainty I am carrying forward rather than resolving: exp_86 does not tell us whether its lift was measured under competitive pressure like today's, so a real recovery in activation may be partly masked by accounts leaving for price reasons — I will read the result against segment-level churn, not headline activation alone. Downstream value risk flagged on two counts: first, simplification must not quietly strip qualifying fields, since fewer required fields at signup can raise completion while degrading lead quality and pushing the revenue cost downstream where this experiment will not see it, so lead-quality and qualified-pipeline metrics are instrumented as guardrails alongside completion; second, the exp_73 finding should be written back to durable memory with its retention caveat intact, so no future session re-derives 'discounting works' from the stripped summary.
